fiber_infrastructure.name: Fiber Infrastructure & Metropolitan Networks
fiber_infrastructure.content: Saudi Arabia possesses an extensive national fiber backbone, with major carriers like STC, Mobily, and Zain KSA driving deployment in line with Vision 2030. Mobily reports over 60,000 km of fiber optic networks. Riyadh is a critical terrestrial hub connecting the Red Sea and Arabian Gulf cable landing stations via diverse, high-capacity DWDM networks. Metropolitan networks in Riyadh are high-density, supporting the deployment of a new LINX-powered IXP and significant FTTH penetration.
key_points: Extensive domestic fiber network with 60,000km+ coverage (Mobily alone).
Riyadh serves as the central terrestrial backbone hub for East-West traffic.
High competition (STC, Mobily, Zain) ensures last-mile redundancy and strong FTTH adoption.

subsea_cables.name: Subsea Cable Infrastructure
subsea_cables.content: The Kingdom is a crucial global transit point, with center3 (STC subsidiary) operating 9 cable landing stations across Jeddah, Yanbu, Duba, Haql, and Al Khobar. Saudi Arabia is connected to 13 in-service subsea cable systems. Key systems include the high-capacity Saudi Vision Cable (SVC) with 18Tbps per fiber pair, 2Africa, SEA-ME-WE 5 (SMW5), and IEX. This diversity on both the Red Sea and Arabian Gulf coasts provides exceptional redundancy and low-latency routing for intercontinental traffic.
key_points: Strategic hub with 9 cable landing stations for maximal geographic diversity.
Connection to 13 in-service subsea cable systems for high redundancy.
New high-capacity cables (SVC) provide up to 288Tbps max capacity per system.

international_connectivity.name: International Connectivity & Global Peering
international_connectivity.content: Saudi Arabia is aggressively developing into the MENA Hub, leveraging its central geographic position to connect Europe, Asia, and Africa. STC's center3 operates international Points of Presence (PoPs) to facilitate global traffic exchange. The multiple diverse cable routes (Red Sea and Arabian Gulf) combined with high-capacity terrestrial links to Riyadh ensure robust and low-latency access to major global markets.
key_points: Designated regional digital hub (MENA Hub) connecting three continents.
High-capacity, diverse route connectivity to Europe and Asia.
Access to global Tier-1 providers via center3's PoPs.

domestic_peering.name: Domestic Peering & Carrier Landscape
domestic_peering.content: The domestic telecommunications market is competitive, dominated by STC (55% market share), Mobily (30%), and Zain KSA (15%). The peering ecosystem is rapidly maturing with multiple IXPs: the government-backed SAIX (Saudi Arabian Internet Exchange) which has a peak traffic of 1.08 Tb/s and 122 connected members, JEDIX (Jeddah IX), and the newly launched LINX-powered Riyadh IX. This growth in local IXPs significantly improves domestic traffic localization and reduces latency for end-users.
key_points: Competitive carrier landscape with three major providers: STC, Mobily, and Zain.
SAIX (1.08 Tb/s peak traffic) and the new Riyadh IX provide strong domestic peering opportunities.
Significant localization of internet traffic is a key focus for low-latency delivery.

latency_performance.name: Latency Performance & CDN Presence
latency_performance.content: Riyadh benefits from KSAs strategic position as a low-latency corridor between Europe and Asia. Domestic fixed broadband latency is competitive, with a reported average as low as 10ms. Major global cloud providers (e.g., Google Cloud, which has joined SAIX) and CDNs have established or are establishing a presence and PoPs to serve the growing regional market. Low RTT to critical global markets is achievable via new high-speed terrestrial fiber from Jeddah/Yanbu.
key_points: Excellent latency for intercontinental traffic (East-West corridor).
Domestic latency is competitive (as low as 10ms).
Major CDN and Cloud providers are actively establishing local PoPs (e.g., Google Cloud joined SAIX).

bandwidth_costs.content: Bandwidth costs are trending toward competitiveness due to increased domestic carrier competition and the high-capacity influx from new subsea cables (e.g., SVC, 2Africa). Scalability is high, with multiple carriers offering dark fiber options, including major deals like the Mobily/Sparkle dark fiber agreement, offering flexible commercial terms and volume discounts.

High scalability and dark fiber options available via major carriers like STC and Mobily.
Inflow of new high-capacity cables (SVC) will continue to drive down unit costs.

STC reports over 85% 5G coverage in populated areas, providing a solid foundation for high-density AI/ML and edge computing workloads. The continuous commissioning of new subsea and terrestrial fiber ensures capacity growth will keep pace with hyperscale demand.

High 5G coverage (85% in populated areas by STC) for edge computing and AI readiness.

temperature_humidity.name: Temperature & Humidity Analysis
temperature_humidity.content: Riyadh has a hot desert climate with extremely high summer temperatures, averaging a maximum of 45C (113F) in July, necessitating robust mechanical cooling. Winter temperatures are mild, with a January night minimum average of 9C (48.2F), offering a substantial diurnal temperature swing and nighttime free-cooling opportunities. The consistently very low relative humidity, dropping to an average of 10-14% in summer, is highly favorable for effective indirect evaporative cooling (IEC) year-round.

Very low annual humidity (10-50%) is ideal for indirect evaporative cooling (IEC).
Significant diurnal temperature variation supports night-time cooling strategies.
Heat stress is the primary operational challenge for equipment efficiency.

cooling_strategy.name: Cooling Strategy & PUE Analysis
cooling_strategy.content: The primary cooling strategy must be a high-efficiency hybrid system, combining mechanical cooling (DX or chiller) for peak summer loads with Indirect Evaporative Cooling (IEC) utilizing the consistently low wet-bulb temperatures. Water-cooled systems may face severe water scarcity challenges. The low humidity allows IEC to significantly reduce the mechanical cooling load, leading to a competitive estimated PUE.
key_points: Hybrid cooling (Mechanical + Indirect Evaporative Cooling) is mandatory.
Estimated PUE of 1.35 is achievable only with aggressive IEC utilization.
High-efficiency mechanical components are required to handle extreme summer heat.
N+N redundancy for cooling infrastructure is critical due to operational extremes.

free_cooling.name: Free Cooling Potential
free_cooling.content: While direct air-side economization is limited by high dry-bulb temperatures, the extremely low wet-bulb temperatures enable high utilization of indirect evaporative cooling. It is estimated that a well-designed IEC system can operate in economization or high-assist mode for over 4,000 hours annually, primarily during the mild winter and night-time, offering significant cost savings over continuous mechanical cooling.
key_points: 4100+ annual hours of economization/assist via Indirect Evaporative Cooling (IEC).
PUE reduction of 0.10 is feasible with optimized IEC deployment.
Direct air-side free cooling is minimal due to high dry-bulb temperatures.

seismic_geological.content: The central Arabian Shield, where Riyadh is located, is classified as having a medium seismic hazard, with relatively low estimated ground motion compared to the active Red Sea coast. There is a 10% chance of potentially damaging earthquake shaking in a 50-year period. Geological stability is generally favorable, but site-specific soil investigation is critical to confirm bearing capacity and rule out liquefaction potential in alluvial deposits along wadis.

Properly engineered foundations are required under Saudi Building Code (SBC) provisions.

hydrological_flood.name: Hydrological & Flood Risk
hydrological_flood.content: The arid climate results in low annual precipitation, but the region is prone to severe flash flooding during rare, intense rainfall events, particularly along the Wadi Hanifa basin which runs through Riyadh. Flood vulnerability is mapped as moderate to high in parts of the urban area. Construction must be sited outside 100-year and 500-year floodplains, utilizing the existing Wadi Hanifa Flood Management Plan which addresses 50-year climate cycle floods. Water scarcity is critical; reliance on municipal or ground water for cooling is a high operational risk.

Water availability for cooling is a major, high-cost operational challenge.
Site elevation and drainage must exceed 500-year flood plain data.

wind_storm.content: Riyadh experiences moderate average wind speeds (12-16 kph), with the windiest part of the year occurring from May to August. Extreme wind events are recorded, with historical maximums around 79.5 km/h. The primary wind-related hazard is the frequency of sand and dust storms, which require advanced air filtration and pressurization systems to protect equipment and maintain PUE efficiency. Structural design must accommodate high wind loads from storms and provide robust sealing.

High-efficiency air filtration (e.g., MERV 16/HEPA) and building pressurization are mandatory.

geopolitical_stability.name: Geopolitical Stability & National Security
geopolitical_stability.content: Saudi Arabia presents a domestically stable political environment, classified in a low-risk category (EKN Country Risk Category 2 of 7 in 2025). The absolute monarchy structure provides political continuity, and the Vision 2030 plan drives major economic diversification and a favorable regulatory environment for foreign investment. However, the operational environment is exposed to high regional geopolitical tensions, particularly with Iran and the ongoing fallout from the Gaza conflict, which introduces potential risk of state-sponsored cyber-attacks against critical infrastructure and supply chain disruption via key maritime chokepoints. Data governance laws require adherence to national security standards (Essential Cybersecurity Controls - ECC) and local data residency rules.

Low sovereign debt and strong currency peg to the US Dollar.
High regional geopolitical exposure introduces external security threats.

infrastructure_resilience.content: The power infrastructure resilience for commercial enterprises is high, with reported power outages in firms in a typical month at 0.000 in December 2022. Local fiber networks benefit from significant 5G and national digital transformation investments, ensuring high redundancy and low latency. economic_social_stability.name: Economic & Social Stability
economic_social_stability.content: The economic profile is strong, underpinned by large oil reserves, low government debt, and a currency pegged to the US Dollar since the mid-1980s. Inflation is stable and low (projected 1.6% in 2024). The 'Vision 2030' program commits substantial sovereign wealth to economic diversification and major infrastructure projects (e.g., mega-projects), creating a favorable environment for foreign direct investment (FDI). Challenges include the heavy reliance on hydrocarbons (over 60% of government revenue), FDI inflows remaining below the 5% GDP target (1.2% in 2023), and a national focus on increasing Saudi labor participation ('Saudization'), which impacts the availability of foreign skilled labor and necessitates focused training programs.

renewable_energy.name: Renewable Energy & Grid Decarbonization
renewable_energy.content: The national grid is currently carbon-intensive, heavily relying on natural gas and liquid fuels, but is undergoing rapid decarbonization under the National Renewable Energy Program (NREP). Vision 2030 targets 50% of power generation from renewables by 2030, supported by an ambitious 130 GW renewable capacity goal. The corporate Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) market is highly active and mature, evidenced by the signing of PPAs for 15 GW of projects involving key international and local players.

High current grid carbon intensity (estimated 450 gCO2/kWh) due to fossil fuel reliance.

carbon_climate_policy.name: Carbon & Climate Policy Framework
carbon_climate_policy.content: Saudi Arabia currently does not impose a mandatory national carbon tax or cap-and-trade system. Climate action is driven by the 2060 Net-Zero goal and the voluntary Greenhouse Gas Crediting and Offsetting Mechanism (GCOM) announced for 2024. The Regional Voluntary Carbon Market Company (RVCMC) launched a carbon exchange platform at COP29, facilitating voluntary offsets. Mandatory climate reporting is currently voluntary for most listed companies but is actively transitioning towards mandatory status under the Capital Market Authority (CMA) and Saudi Exchange guidelines.
key_points: No mandatory carbon tax in place, keeping immediate operating costs low.
Developing voluntary carbon market (GCOM, RVCMC) offers offset opportunities.
Mandatory climate reporting expected to be embedded in governance rules soon.

environmental_regulations.name: Environmental & Resource Regulations
environmental_regulations.content: Environmental Impact Assessments (EIAs) are mandatory via a detailed Environmental Compliance Form (ECF) submitted to the National Center for Environmental Compliance (NCEC), covering water use, energy, and emissions. Water scarcity is the critical constraint, with data center consumption projected to grow by 34.1% CAGR. Data centers primarily rely on energy-intensive desalinated water. Regulations exist for waste/pollution control and a '30% by 30 Plan' commits to protecting 30% of land/marine areas by 2030.
key_points: Mandatory Environmental Compliance Form (ECF) for large projects.
Critical water scarcity risk due to reliance on energy-intensive desalination.
Future water efficiency and reuse standards are a compliance priority.

social_community_impact.name: Social & Community Impact Assessment
social_community_impact.content: The government enforces strict 'Saudization' (local hiring) and Local Content policies, particularly for entities dealing with State-Owned Enterprises (SOEs) like STC, requiring local sourcing of goods and services. Recent labor law reforms have improved the mobility and rights of foreign workers, enhancing fairness. Public perception is generally supportive of digital infrastructure due to its alignment with Vision 2030's economic diversification goals, but community opposition to water-intensive projects is a latent risk.
key_points: Mandatory Local Content and Saudization policies require strategic local engagement.
Recent labor law reforms enhance worker rights and reduce social risk from labor practices.
Strong national policy alignment for tech infrastructure development (Vision 2030).

The Saudi Exchange (formerly Tadawul) issued voluntary ESG disclosure guidelines in 2021, and a set of 29 Unified ESG Metrics for GCC was adopted in 2023. Compliance is voluntary but is a de facto necessity for attracting foreign investment and is moving toward mandatory status. The Data Centers Services Regulations (DCSR), effective 2024, mandates stringent technical and cybersecurity governance (Tier, ISO/IEC 27001, NCA), creating a robust regulatory environment for data center operations.
key_points: Robust Data Centers Services Regulations (DCSR) ensure high operational and security governance.
Voluntary ESG reporting is rapidly maturing towards a mandatory framework.
Alignment with international standards (GRI, SASB, ISO) is a regulatory expectation.

competitive_landscape.content: Riyadh is a Tier-1 emerging hyperscale market, experiencing a rapid influx of investment driven by Saudi Vision 2030. The market is transitioning from local colocation to massive hyperscale self-builds and wholesale colocation. The primary competitive dynamic is the race between major hyperscalers (AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Oracle) to establish sovereign cloud regions, which is driving up competition for land and utility capacity. The market is highly under-supplied relative to the national 2030 digital ambition, leading to high projected absorption rates for new capacity.

peering_opportunities.name: Peering Opportunities & Network Ecosystem
peering_opportunities.content: The network ecosystem is developing rapidly, positioning Saudi Arabia as a crucial East-West connectivity hub. The government-backed Saudi Arabian Internet Exchange (SAIX) in Riyadh, with its multi-Terabit capacity, provides excellent local peering. The country's strong submarine cable infrastructure and numerous upcoming cable landings bolster its international gateway status, vital for hyperscaler long-haul network strategies.

The concentration of global/regional HQs (e.g., Lenovo, Amazon, Google) in areas like King Abdullah Financial District (KAFD) ensures a high-quality customer pipeline.

labor_market.content: The technical labor market is in a rapid growth phase, supported by heavy government investment in upskilling programs aligned with Vision 2030. While talent is in high demand and salaries for specialized roles (like Data Scientist, ~$112,000/year) are competitive, the overall cost base is lower than traditional Tier-1 hyperscale hubs. The 25% Saudization requirement in the IT sector creates a necessary focus on local workforce development and training partnerships for hyperscalers.

Challenges include the high OPEX of cooling in a desert climate, driving innovation toward liquid cooling, and the need for significant, committed power infrastructure for multi-phase, multi-hundred-MW deployments.

The consistently low ambient humidity throughout the year presents a unique climate opportunity, enabling aggressive utilization of Indirect Evaporative Cooling (IEC) for over 4,000 annual hours of assistance, which, despite the severe heat, provides a critical lever for achieving competitive Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) metrics compared to other hot, humid coastal regions.

Domestic political stability is very high, reinforced by a robust economic profile and low inflation, which provides a strong, predictable financial foundation for long-term CapEx investment, offsetting the high regional geopolitical risks and supporting project financing confidence.
key_challenges: The critical lack of confirmed power details (allocation, cost, reliability specifics) combined with the high seasonal grid strain risk during extreme summer heat (Risk Analysis) represents the single greatest critical path constraint, requiring immediate, Tier IV level redundancy planning and negotiation for guaranteed capacity allocation to proceed.

The interdependence of extreme heat (Climate Analysis) and severe water scarcity (ESG Analysis) mandates costly, water-efficient cooling systems (e.g., optimized dry cooling/IEC), leading to significant CapEx inflation and high operational risk until a firm, non-potable water supply contract or advanced recycling facility is secured and permitted via the mandatory Environmental Compliance Form (ECF).

Regulatory mandates for strict data localization (PDPL) combined with the Local Content policy and Saudization requirements (ESG Analysis) create significant friction in the operational phase, requiring specialized sovereign cloud architectural design and substantial investment in training local talent, increasing both OpEx and human resources complexity.

The current high-carbon intensity of the national grid (ESG Analysis) forces immediate, large-scale engagement in the mature Corporate Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) market to align with global decarbonization targets and mitigate reputational risk, adding immediate complexity and financial commitment to the energy strategy.
strategic_opportunities: Establish a premium 'Sovereign Interconnection Hub' leveraging the world-class network diversity (13+ cables) and mandated data localization (PDPL), differentiating the facility as the essential point for both highly compliant local data storage and low-latency international transit across Europe, Asia, and Africa.

Utilize the mature Saudi PPA market and Vision 2030s 50% renewable energy target to negotiate a long-term, fixed-price renewable energy contract, locking in predictable, lower-carbon OpEx that provides a significant competitive advantage over facilities relying solely on the volatile, high-carbon utility grid.

Leverage the location's industrial zoning to streamline permitting processes and access high-voltage substations, accelerating the physical construction start timeline compared to dense urban core developments, while simultaneously positioning the facility to serve hyper-density AI/ML workloads supported by the aggressive 5G coverage (Network Analysis).

Target government and State-Owned Enterprise (SOE) clients by proactively designing the facility to meet the Essential Cybersecurity Controls (ECC) and NCA standards outlined in the Risk Analysis, fulfilling local content mandates, thus unlocking access to high-value, long-term contracts restricted by regulatory policy.
critical_success_factors: Immediate closure of the power capacity agreement, including securing a high-priority, dedicated high-voltage feed and establishing redundant internal power generation (2N or better) to counteract the seasonal grid vulnerability identified in the Risk Analysis.

Finalizing the cooling system design (CapEx-heavy, low-water use hybrid system) and securing the Environmental Compliance Form (ECF) approval based on confirmed water sourcing (e.g., treated sewage effluent or advanced recycling) to break ground and mitigate permitting delays.

Developing a comprehensive sovereign architecture and compliance framework that explicitly satisfies PDPL requirements for data residency and the NCA's cybersecurity mandates, enabling the capture of premium government and regulated sector workloads.

Implementing a proactive, multi-phased Saudization and Local Content program early in the project lifecycle to ensure labor compliance and unlock necessary government incentives and strategic local partnerships mandated by the ESG and Regulatory domains.

phase_1_deployment.recommended_capacity: The initial phase should target 12 Megawatts (MW) of critical IT load capacity, constrained primarily by the unconfirmed power allocation and the high CapEx requirement for cooling and resilience infrastructure. This capacity allows sufficient volume to justify the substantial investment in carrier-neutral interconnection facilities and advanced water-efficient cooling systems, while ensuring the site remains modularly scalable to 48+ MW once power certainty is achieved.
phase_1_deployment.timeline: The projected timeline for Ready-For-Service (RFS) is 26 to 30 months, significantly extended due to the mandatory 6-9 month pre-construction phase dedicated entirely to power confirmation, water solution engineering, and navigating the Environmental Compliance Form (ECF) process. Construction starts only after the power allocation and environmental approval are secured, mitigating the highest cross-domain regulatory and utility risks.
priority_actions: Immediately engage the Saudi Electricity Company (SEC) and relevant regulators to finalize the guaranteed power allocation contract, confirming the specific high-voltage connection point, negotiating unit pricing, and establishing terms for mitigating seasonal brownout risk, treating this as the non-negotiable Critical Path Item Number One.

Appoint specialized environmental and cooling engineers to design a validated, minimal-water-use hybrid cooling solution (optimized IEC/Dry Coolers) and proactively submit the mandatory Environmental Compliance Form (ECF), demonstrating secured non-potable water sourcing to satisfy the severe water scarcity constraints identified in the Climate and ESG domains.

Develop the legal and technical compliance architecture, specifically designing the operational stack and facility layout to achieve full ISO/IEC 27001 certification and PDPL compliance for sovereign data segregation, ensuring readiness to onboard high-value regulated tenants immediately upon launch.

Initiate the Corporate Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) negotiation process immediately to secure 100% renewable energy sourcing, effectively locking in long-term OpEx predictability and mitigating the reputational risk associated with the current high-carbon grid intensity before the facility becomes operational.
phase_1_deployment.estimated_investment: The estimated initial investment for the 12 MW facility is projected to be in the range of $180 Million to $220 Million USD, reflecting a premium TCO per kW due to the mandatory CapEx inflation driven by Tier IV power redundancy, specialized climate resilience hardening (anti-sandstorm filtration, oversized mechanical cooling), and highly efficient, low-water cooling infrastructure required by the Climate and Risk analyses.
risk_mitigation: Mitigate high regional geopolitical risk by implementing advanced, multi-layered physical security protocols (Tier IV standard), including specialized access controls and counter-surveillance measures, and establishing a robust cybersecurity framework compliant with NCAs Essential Cybersecurity Controls (ECC).

Address the long-term climate change vulnerability by engineering cooling infrastructure to operate reliably up to 55 Celsius (9C buffer above current extremes), incorporating redundancy and durability that ensures the facility's 30-year operational lifespan is not compromised by the projected increase in extreme heat days.

Counter the friction from Saudization policies by establishing immediate partnerships with local technical training institutions, developing a clear pipeline for localizing skilled roles (HR and technical operations), and integrating Local Content mandates into the core supply chain bidding process.

Mitigate flash flood risk (Climate Analysis) by mandating that the facility's finished floor elevation and critical infrastructure placement must exceed the projected 500-year floodplain data and implementing robust site-specific drainage and hydrological management systems.

Negotiate a detailed service level agreement (SLA) with multiple network providers (STC, Mobily, Zain) offering diverse entry points and redundant terrestrial fiber paths, utilizing the competitive carrier landscape (Network Analysis) to ensure network resilience against physical cuts or localized carrier outages.
success_metrics: Achieve power procurement certainty, measured by a signed, guaranteed 12 MW power allocation contract with SEC within 6 months of project initiation, confirming acceptable unit costs and clear seasonal supply risk mitigation terms.

Attain environmental compliance success, quantified by securing the final Environmental Compliance Form (ECF) approval from NCEC within 9 months, specifically verifying the viability and permitting of the water-efficient cooling strategy.

Demonstrate operational resilience by maintaining an average annual PUE below 1.45, measured monthly, achieved through the optimal deployment and continuous utilization of the high-efficiency Indirect Evaporative Cooling (IEC) system despite the extreme summer heat.

Attain a 100% network uptime SLA achievement, measured quarterly, leveraging the high carrier diversity and redundant intercontinental connectivity inherent in the location's strategic network hub status.

insights_result.strategic_recommendation: The comprehensive strategic recommendation is to proceed with the investment, but under a highly risk-controlled, phased approach that front-loads critical utility and regulatory compliance requirements. The unique combination of world-class network connectivity and robust regulatory governance (DCSR) provides a compelling competitive advantage that justifies the high CapEx. The deployment strategy must be built on securing long-term renewable PPAs and engineering a hyper-resilient, water-minimal facility, effectively converting the local climate and ESG challenges into proprietary technical advantages that are difficult for competitors to replicate. Success is contingent upon treating the Power and Water solutions as co-dependent critical path constraints that must be resolved before significant construction expenditure.
insights_result.conclusion: GO recommendation with high confidence (85% confidence level), contingent upon the successful resolution of the power allocation and water management strategy within the first nine months. The Riyadh 2 location offers unparalleled access to the highly valuable Saudi enterprise market and functions as an essential, regulated interconnection gateway for global East-West traffic. Failure to secure the definitive power supply or approval for a sustainable water-use strategy would immediately reduce the confidence level and potentially trigger a no-go reassessment due to unmanageable OpEx and resilience risk. Key success factors include maintaining stringent physical and cyber security (ECC/NCA compliance), achieving rapid deployment of the low-carbon PPA, and ensuring technical readiness for PDPL-mandated sovereign workloads.
next_steps: Convene a dedicated, high-level negotiation team focused exclusively on securing the high-priority, guaranteed electrical capacity agreement with SEC and concurrently begin formal PPA negotiations with major renewable energy developers in the Kingdom to lock in long-term renewable supply.

Initiate the procurement of critical long-lead-time cooling infrastructure components immediately after the final cooling design is approved, recognizing the specialized nature of high-temperature, low-water-use systems required to operate reliably under extreme long-term climate projections.

Engage local counsel and specialized compliance consultants to architect the legal entity structure and operational framework necessary to satisfy both PDPL data localization requirements and the mandatory Saudization and Local Content policies for all subcontracts and hiring.

Finalize the site geotechnical survey and detailed engineering design for the facilitys foundations, ensuring full compliance with the Saudi Building Code (SBC) and incorporating necessary hardening against sandstorms, flash flooding, and potential high wind events.
